extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and in-house patent counsel drafting and prosecuting AI-related patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Best-practice guidance for preparing, drafting, prosecuting, and enforcing patent applications covering artificial intelligence inventions, including disclosure interviewing, specification drafting for §101/§112, claim strategies, detectability/trade-secret considerations, ethics, and international differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set the Context (identify invention aspect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the AI invention is directed to training method, inference method, architecture, application, or multiple aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding which aspect(s) the invention targets sets the stage for the disclosure interview and subsequent drafting. Example: pruning or reward-function tuning focuses on training; novel use-cases of a conventionally trained network focus on inference. Interview prompt: 'Does the AI invention relate to data collection, data pre-processing, training, inference, or the underlying AI architecture?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the Problem (technical challenge & solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the invention in terms of the technical challenge it addresses and the technical solution it provides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing is useful for novelty/non-obviousness (35 U.S.C. §§102/103) and subject-matter eligibility (§101). Ask inventors what technical challenges they faced, unexpected problems, and why conventional approaches were inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify Technical Advantages (show technical improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Document how the AI invention provides technical improvements to the challenged problem (e.g., improves functioning of a computer, device, or technical field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements need not be over well-understood/conventional activities; they need only improve functioning (efficiency, accuracy, speed, resource use). Provide concrete examples (e.g., design enabling operation on edge device) and claim architectural aspects to show non-conventionality. Useful when arguing integration of a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A, prong II of USPTO test).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand System Inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what kinds of data are used as inputs to the system and what data are used for training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify distinctions between data used to develop/train a model and data used at inference time. Interview prompt: 'What kind of data is used as input to the system? What kind of data is used for training the system?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the Data and Data Collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain detailed information on the nature, organization, volume, sources, and methods of obtaining training and input data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether data are organized as objects/attributes, possible names/values, sample sizes, source provenance, and collection methods; these details support enablement and can expose ethical/data-bias issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand Pre-processing Steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and describe any data pre-processing applied before model training or inference and whether such pre-processing is conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if pre-processing seems peripheral, document types (normalizing, filtering, segmentation, geometric transforms, super-resolution, etc.) and whether pre-processing involves more than conventional computer processing; consider whether pre-processing contributes to inventive concept or technical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand Post-processing Steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe any processing performed on the AI output to make it usable, and identify what components perform post-processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document transformations, additional processing pipelines, devices/systems used for post-processing, and whether post-processing contributes to technical improvement or enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand Network Architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe high-level architecture (CNN, RNN, transformers, etc.), the structure of individual layers, activation functions, layer interconnections, and integration with system context (sensors, user devices, databases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detail how architectural elements relate to the problem solved; identify multiple architectures if combined; document per-layer structure, activation functions, connections, and the overall computing environment to support enablement and eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the Training Process
rubrics_metrics.description: Document training paradigms (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement), training data, loss functions, optimization algorithms, hyperparameters, staged training, pruning, and which parts of networks are trained or fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training details can affect eligibility (training claims sometimes easier to show eligible), enforceability (detection/split-infringement issues), and enablement. Interview prompts: 'What loss function(s) are used?' 'What optimization algorithm?' 'What hyperparameters?' 'Are parts trained separately or jointly?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the Process at Inference Time
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe inputs and outputs during inference, the enabling architecture, improvements resulting from inference, whether trained models are updated at inference, and whether input data distributions change over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify how inference is carried out, how outputs are made usable, whether models are retrained or updated online, and whether combining models or multi-network arrangements are employed; these support claim drafting on inference and enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical Risk Identification (bias, privacy, exploitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify ethical risks including statistical bias, disproportionate impacts on demographics, privacy concerns, and potential malicious exploitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because AI systems are data-driven, incomplete/biased data can cause discriminatory outcomes or privacy violations. Patent counsel should spot potential ethics issues at disclosure to allow mitigation or referral to ethics teams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Counsel Role in Promoting Ethical AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent counsel should flag ethics concerns, gather additional information, connect inventors with AI ethics partners, and conduct discussions (not lectures) to surface and mitigate risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor involvement by invention type (technical determinations vs. social determinations). Counsel can run ethical risk measurement exercises or reserve part of inventor interviews for ethical discussions; avoid non-technical buzzwords and respect technical partners' perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO Drafting Considerations (technical problem/solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing to the EPO, clearly define the technical problem and the technical solution; features related to the technical solution may be required in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO treats computational models/algorithms as abstract per se; to obtain a patent, show application to solve a technical problem in a field of technology. Draft specification and claims to emphasize technical application and include technical features in claims where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Korean Enablement/Eligibility Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Korean practice may be less stringent on eligibility if a technical idea is embodied in a computer; enablement may require description of correlation between input and output data from a trained model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include descriptions of learning data, correlations between data and solutions, and how a trained model is generated from input data to satisfy Korean enablement requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Japanese Enablement and Support Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: JPO expects specification to enable creation of a learned model achieving a certain degree of accuracy; disclose relationships between input and output data used in training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete relationships (e.g., correlations) between features and outputs and evidence or explanation supporting the claimed accuracy; avoid only high-level or vague feature descriptions that fail support/enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese Claim/Description Guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Chinese Guidelines require considering claims as a whole; show algorithmic adjustments that provide technical effects; written description should show how technical features interact and include practical application (input/output).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims and spec to present technical features collectively, include input parameters and outputs tied to specific technical areas, and explain interactions between features. Objective user-experience improvements should be grounded in technical implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship Jurisdictional Awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that many jurisdictions currently require natural persons as inventors (AI generally not acceptable as named inventor in many countries); monitor litigation and jurisdiction-specific outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace conception to human contributors, avoid naming AI as inventor in jurisdictions that disallow it, and consider choice of filing jurisdictions if AI-generated inventions raise novel inventorship questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace Conception to Human Inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Document and trace how potentially novel aspects have human contributors and prepare to name humans who contributed to what is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants are advised to avoid listing AI as inventor and to collect evidence of human conception to withstand inventorship challenges until laws evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting to Prevent or Overcome §101 Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft AI applications to show patent-eligible subject matter by integrating any alleged judicial exception into a practical application and by claiming AI-specific architecture or training elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use USPTO examples (e.g., Example 39) as guidance: emphasize technical improvements, specific implementations, and avoid purely abstract high-level claims. Show how claims improve computing/technical fields (efficiency, accuracy, speed, resource use) and avoid preemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claiming Strategies (architecture, training, problem/solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ claim types such as architecture claims, training claims, and problem/solution claims to capture AI-specific innovations and enhance eligibility/enforceability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architecture and training claims can emphasize tangible technical elements; problem/solution claims tie claim scope to a technical problem and practical effect. Consider inclusion of architectural details, training steps, loss functions, data flows, and interactions with devices/endpoints in claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art Unit Selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider prosecution art unit selection strategically to improve examination outcomes for AI-related claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different USPTO art units may apply subject-matter eligibility analysis differently; selecting an appropriate art unit that recognizes AI technical improvements may help avoid adverse examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding §112 Rejections (enablement & written description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft the specification to satisfy §112 by providing sufficient disclosure of architecture, training, and problem/solution detail to enable a person skilled in the art to practice the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go beyond high-level descriptions: disclose lower levels of abstraction (layers, nodes, activation functions), training paradigms, training data relationships, loss functions and hyperparameters, and how features interact to solve a technical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture Description for Enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide detailed architecture descriptions including layer structure, node behavior, activation functions, and inter-layer connectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement benefits from lower-level operational details rather than only high-level labels (e.g., 'image classification'); such details help satisfy enablement and written description and support eligibility arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training Description for Enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose training details including training data, loss functions, optimization algorithms, hyperparameters, staged training/pruning/refinement, and which parts of the network are trained or fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because AI inventions often rely on training data, describing how models are trained and how input correlates to output supports enablement and may be required in some jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem/Solution Support in Specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly set out the technical problem and the concrete technical solution in the specification to support claims and to satisfy foreign office expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document how claimed features solve the technical problem, how features interact to produce effects, and, where possible, quantify improvements (accuracy, speed, resource usage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting to Withstand Appellate/CAFC Scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare specifications and claims with sufficient technical specificity and factual record to defend subject-matter eligibility and other challenges on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on USPTO guidance (not precedential); anticipate Federal Circuit focus on concrete technical improvements and avoid conflating novelty with eligibility. Provide factual allegations of technical improvement where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims and Detectability / Trade Secret Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether claimed features are detectable when an accused product is operated, whether features are disclosed publicly, and whether claims will undermine trade-secret protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify 'detectable features', features likely viewable during operation, and those that competitors may publicly disclose. If features are reverse-engineerable or standard-compliant, they may not be maintainable as trade secrets—adjust claiming strategy accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cloud-Based / As-a-Service (aaS) Documentation Paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Include specification language addressing cloud-based implementations and documentation practices for aaS deployments to clarify how the claimed invention operates when remotely implemented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documenting cloud interactions, endpoints, and data flows in the specification supports enablement and helps with detectability/enforcement where the core operation is remote or distributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Claiming Features Likely Disclosed Publicly
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious claiming features that are very likely to be disclosed in competitors’ public documents or standards, which can affect enforceability and trade-secret strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If features are standard-compliant or publicly documented, consider different claim scopes or focusing on combinations/implementations that produce technical improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document Interactions and Data Flows for Enablement & Detectability
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify how the inventive system interacts with and acquires data from sources and endpoint devices and how data flows are arranged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed descriptions of data acquisition, endpoints, user interactions, and data flows support enablement and can aid downstream detectability and enforcement analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate Non-Preemptive Technical Improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Show how claimed innovations enhance computing systems or AI systems (efficiency, accuracy, speed, resource use) in a manner that does not preempt fundamental methods or abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete implementation details and measurable or concrete effects; avoid overly broad claim language that could be characterized as preemptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage USPTO Examples and PTAB Decisions with Caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Use USPTO PEG examples (e.g., Example 39) and PTAB informative decisions (e.g., Ex Parte Hannun) as drafting guidance but recognize they are not precedential in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO materials can illustrate claim/spec drafting approaches that succeeded at the Office, but litigation outcomes are governed by Federal Circuit and Supreme Court precedent—draft to survive both examination and judicial scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor Recent Case Law and District Court Trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware district courts have shown mixed results on computer/AI eligibility; many AI-related patents were invalidated early, but outcomes vary based on claim specificity and alleged technical improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case examples (e.g., Smart Systems, Athena Diagnostics, Singular Computing, Applied Predictive Techs., Kaavo) to inform drafting: courts favor claims with plausible technical improvements and specific implementations; pleadings with factual allegations of improvement may survive early dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate Ethical Considerations into Practice
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions that implicate privacy, bias, or social impacts, proactively incorporate ethical analysis into patent practice and connect with product/ethics stakeholders as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical assessment may influence design choices, specification content, or even the decision to pursue patenting; counsel can help surface potential issues and recommend mitigations or cross-team collaboration.
